ukberi-tibyan:24-24.t:
Allah the Exalted says: (فَإِنْ لَمْ تَفْعَلُوا وَلَنْ تَفْعَلُوا فَاتَّقُوا النَّارَ الَّتِي وَقُودُهَا النَّاسُ وَالْحِجَارَةُ أُعِدَّتْ لِلْكَافِرِينَ (٢٤)).
His saying, Exalted is He: (فَإِنْ لَمْ تَفْعَلُوا): the jussive (jazm) is caused by لم, not by إن, because ((لم)) is an operator very closely joined to what it governs, and it occurs only with a verb that is imperfect in form, whereas إن has entered on a verb that is past in form, and a noun has followed it directly, as in His saying, Exalted is He: (وَإِنْ أَحَدٌ مِنَ الْمُشْرِكِينَ).
(وَقُودُهَا النَّاسُ): the majority read it with fatḥa on the wāw, and it means firewood; it has also been read with ḍamma, which is a dialectal variant for firewood. The better view is that it is a maṣdar (verbal noun) meaning "burning", and that there is an omitted muḍāf in the speech, its implied form being: "its burning is the burning of people", or "the blazing of people", or "possessed of that whose fuel is people".
(أُعِدَّتْ): a clause in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial) from النار, and its operator is فاتقوا.
It is not permissible for it to be a ḥāl from the pronoun in «وقودها» for three reasons: first, that it is a muḍāf ilayhi; second, that firewood does not govern a ḥāl; third, that you would be separating the maṣdar, or what operates like it, from what it governs by the khabar (predicate), which is الناس.

ukberi-tibyan:25-25.t:
Allah the Exalted says: (وَبَشِّرِ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ أَنَّ لَهُمْ جَنَّاتٍ تَجْرِي مِنْ تَحْتِهَا الْأَنْهَارُ كُلَّمَا رُزِقُوا مِنْهَا مِنْ ثَمَرَةٍ رِزْقًا قَالُوا هَذَا الَّذِي رُزِقْنَا مِنْ قَبْلُ وَأُتُوا بِهِ مُتَشَابِهًا وَلَهُمْ فِيهَا أَزْوَاجٌ مُطَهَّرَةٌ وَهُمْ فِيهَا خَالِدُونَ (٢٥)).
His saying, Exalted is He: (أَنَّ لَهُمْ جَنَّاتٍ): (أنّ) takes fatḥa here because the implied form is بأنّ لهم ("that they have"), and the position of أنّ together with what it governs is accusative (naṣb) by بشّر, because when the preposition is omitted the verb reaches [its object] by itself. This is the doctrine of Sībawayh.
Al-Khalīl allowed it to be in the position of the genitive (jarr) by the omitted bāʾ, because this is a position in which it is added, so it is as if it were pronounced. That is not permissible with anything other than أنّ: if you said بشّره بأنه مخلّد في الجنة ("give him the glad tidings that he will be immortal in Paradise"), omitting the bāʾ would be permissible because of the length of the speech, but if you said بشّره الخلودَ it would not be permissible. This is a principle that recurs very often in the Qur'an, so reflect on it and look for it here. (تَجْرِي مِنْ تَحْتِهَا الْأَنْهَارُ): the clause is in the position of the accusative as a ṣifa (adjective) of الجنات, and الأنهار is nominative by (تجري), not by being a mubtadaʾ (subject) with من تحتها as the khabar (predicate), nor by تحتها, because تجري contains no pronoun, since the gardens do not flow; only their rivers flow. The implied form is "from beneath its trees", not "from beneath its ground", and the muḍāf was omitted.
If it were said that الجنة is the trees themselves, so that there is no omission in the speech, that would be a valid view.
(كُلَّمَا رُزِقُوا مِنْهَا...) up to His saying (مِنْ قَبْلُ) is in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial) from الذين آمنوا, its implied form being: "continually provided for". It may also be a ḥāl from الجنات, because they have been described and the clause contains a pronoun referring back to them, namely His saying: منها. (رُزِقْنَا مِنْ قَبْلُ): that is, رُزِقناه ("we were provided with it"), and the referring pronoun (ʿāʾid) was omitted. قبلُ is indeclinable (mabnī) because it is cut off from the iḍāfa, since the implied form is من قبلِ هذا ("before this").
(وَأُتُوا بِهِ): it may be a ḥāl, with قد intended along with it, its implied form being: "they said that, and they had been given it". It may also be resumptive. And (مُتَشَابِهًا) is a ḥāl from the hāʾ in به. (وَلَهُمْ فِيهَا أَزْوَاجٌ): أزواج is the mubtadaʾ, لهم is the khabar, and فيها is an adverbial (ẓarf) of the [implied] istiqrār ("being settled"). فيها cannot be the khabar, because the benefit [of the statement] would be diminished, since the benefit lies in making the spouses theirs. The second (فيها) is attached to «خالدون». These two clauses are resumptive. The second may also be a ḥāl from the hāʾ and mīm in لهم, its operator being the meaning of istiqrār.

ukberi-tibyan:26-26.t:
Allah the Exalted says: (إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يَسْتَحْيِي أَنْ يَضْرِبَ مَثَلًا مَا بَعُوضَةً فَمَا فَوْقَهَا فَأَمَّا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا فَيَعْلَمُونَ أَنَّهُ الْحَقُّ مِنْ رَبِّهِمْ وَأَمَّا الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا فَيَقُولُونَ مَاذَا أَرَادَ اللَّهُ بِهَذَا مَثَلًا يُضِلُّ بِهِ كَثِيرًا وَيَهْدِي بِهِ كَثِيرًا وَمَا يُضِلُّ بِهِ إِلَّا الْفَاسِقِينَ (٢٦)).
His saying, Exalted is He: (لَا يَسْتَحْيِي): its pattern is يستفعل; no verb from it is used without the sīn, and its meaning is not that of seeking [as the istafʿala pattern often implies]. Its second and third radicals (ʿayn and lām) are both yāʾ, and its root is الحياء ("modesty"); the hamza of الحياء replaces a yāʾ.
In an irregular (shādhdh) reading it was read يستحي, with a single yāʾ; the omitted one is the lām, as it is omitted in the jussive, and on this reading its pattern is يستفِع, except that the yāʾ had its vowel transferred to the ʿayn and became quiescent. It has also been said that the omitted letter is the ʿayn, but that is far-fetched. (أَنْ يَضْرِبَ): that is, من أن يضرب; so its position is accusative according to Sībawayh and genitive according to al-Khalīl.
(مَا): a redundant (zāʾida) particle for emphasis, and «بعوضة» is a badal (substitute) from مثلا.
It has also been said: (ما) is an indefinite noun qualified by an adjective (nakira mawṣūfa), and بعوضة is a badal from ما.
It is read irregularly as بعوضةٌ, in the nominative, on the basis that ما is taken in the sense of الذي and the mubtadaʾ is omitted, i.e. "that which is a gnat". It is also possible that ما is a particle and the mubtadaʾ is implied, its implied form being: "a parable, it being a gnat". (فَمَا فَوْقَهَا): the fāʾ is for conjunction, and ما is an indefinite noun qualified by an adjective or equivalent to الذي; the operator in فوق on both views is the [implied] istiqrār, and what it is conjoined to is بعوضة.
(أَمَّا): a particle standing in for the conditional particle and the protasis (fiʿl al-sharṭ). It is mentioned to detail what was stated in summary; the noun after it occurs as a mubtadaʾ (subject), and the fāʾ is obligatory on its khabar (predicate). The original form is مهما يكن من شيء فالذين آمنوا يعلمون ("whatever the case may be, those who believe know"); but since أمّا stands in for the conditional particle, they disliked placing the fāʾ directly after it, so they deferred it to the khabar, and the mention of the mubtadaʾ after it became a compensation for pronouncing the protasis. (مِنْ رَبِّهِمْ): in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial). The implied form is: "that it is established" or "settled from their Lord", and the operator is the meaning of الحق; the one to whom the ḥāl refers is the latent (mustatir) pronoun in it. (مَاذَا): there are two views on it. First: that «ما» is an interrogative noun whose position is nominative as a mubtadaʾ, ذا is in the sense of الذي, and أراد is its ṣila (relative clause), the referring pronoun being omitted; الذي with its ṣila is the khabar of the mubtadaʾ.
Second: that ما and ذا form a single interrogative noun whose position is accusative by (أراد), with no pronoun in the verb; the implied form is: "what thing did Allah intend?". (مَثَلًا): a tamyīz (specification), i.e. "in terms of a parable". It may also be a ḥāl from هذا, i.e. "being presented as a parable" (mutamaththilan), or "being cited as a parable" (mutamaththalan bihi), in which case it is a ḥāl from the name of Allah. (يُضِلُّ): it may be in the position of the accusative as a ṣifa (adjective) of المثل; it may be a ḥāl from the name of Allah; and it may be resumptive. (إِلَّا الْفَاسِقِينَ): the mafʿūl bihi (direct object) of يضل, and it is not accusative as an excepted noun, because يضل had not taken its object before إلا.

ukberi-tibyan:27-27.t:
Allah the Exalted says: (الَّذِينَ يَنْقُضُونَ عَهْدَ اللَّهِ مِنْ بَعْدِ مِيثَاقِهِ وَيَقْطَعُونَ مَا أَمَرَ اللَّهُ بِهِ أَنْ يُوصَلَ وَيُفْسِدُونَ فِي الْأَرْضِ أُولَئِكَ هُمُ الْخَاسِرُونَ (٢٧)).
His saying, Exalted is He: (الَّذِينَ يَنْقُضُونَ): in the position of the accusative as a ṣifa (adjective) of الفاسقين.
It may also be accusative by an implied أعني ("I mean"), or nominative as a khabar (predicate), i.e. "they are those who".
It may also be a mubtadaʾ (subject), with the khabar being His saying: أولئك هم الخاسرون.
(مِنْ بَعْدِ): من is for the beginning of the extent of time, according to the view of those who allow that, and redundant (zāʾida) according to the view of those who do not allow it; but this is problematic on the latter's own principle, because he does not allow من to be redundant in an affirmative statement.
(مِيثَاقِهِ): a maṣdar (verbal noun) in the sense of الإيثاق ("binding by covenant"). The hāʾ refers to the name of Allah or to العهد. If you refer it to the name of Allah, the maṣdar is annexed to its agent; if you refer it to العهد, it is annexed to its object.
(مَا أَمَرَ): ما is in the sense of الذي, and it may also be an indefinite noun qualified by an adjective. «أن يوصل» is in the position of the genitive as a badal (substitute) from the hāʾ, i.e. "[commanded] its being joined". It may also be a badal from ما, a badal of inclusion (badal al-ishtimāl), its implied form being: "and they sever the joining of what Allah commanded".
It may also be in the position of the nominative, i.e. "it is that it be joined".
(أُولَئِكَ) is a mubtadaʾ; «هم» is a second mubtadaʾ or a separating pronoun (faṣl), and «الخاسرون» is the khabar.

ukberi-tibyan:28-28.t:
Allah the Exalted says: (كَيْفَ تَكْفُرُونَ بِاللَّهِ وَكُنْتُمْ أَمْوَاتًا فَأَحْيَاكُمْ ثُمَّ يُمِيتُكُمْ ثُمَّ يُحْيِيكُمْ ثُمَّ إِلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ) ((٢٨)).
His saying, Exalted is He: (كَيْفَ تَكْفُرُونَ بِاللَّهِ): كيف is in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial), and the operator in it is تكفرون; the one to whom the ḥāl refers is the pronoun in «تكفرون», and the like. [Translator's note: the Arabic reads «والعامل في تكفرون», apparently for «والعامل فيه تكفرون»; translated according to the evident sense.] And (تكفرون) is made transitive by a preposition, but it has been made transitive by itself in His saying: (أَلَا إِنَّ عَادًا كَفَرُوا رَبَّهُمْ); that is construed according to the meaning, since the meaning is "they denied". (وَكُنْتُمْ): «قد» is implied along with it, and the clause is a ḥāl.
(ثُمَّ إِلَيْهِ): the hāʾ is the pronoun of the name of Allah. It may also be the pronoun of the giving of life, indicated by His saying: فأحياكم.

ukberi-tibyan:29-29.t:
Allah the Exalted says: (هُوَ الَّذِي خَلَقَ لَكُمْ مَا فِي الْأَرْضِ جَمِيعًا ثُمَّ اسْتَوَى إِلَى السَّمَاءِ فَسَوَّاهُنَّ سَبْعَ سَمَوَاتٍ وَهُوَ بِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ عَلِيمٌ) (٢٩).
His saying, Exalted is He: (جَمِيعًا): a ḥāl (circumstantial) in the sense of مجتمعا ("all together"). (فَسَوَّاهُنَّ): the pronoun is plural only because السماء is the plural of سماوة; the wāw in it was changed to hamza because it occurred word-finally after an extra alif. (سَبْعَ سَمَوَاتٍ): سبع is accusative as a badal (substitute) from the pronoun. It has also been said that the implied form is: "so He fashioned of them seven heavens", as in His saying: (وَاخْتَارَ مُوسَى قَوْمَهُ), so it would be a mafʿūl bihi (direct object). It has also been said that سوّى is in the sense of صيّر ("made into"), so it would be a second object. (وَهُوَ): it is read with the hāʾ made quiescent, though its original vowel is ḍamma; it was made quiescent only because it became like عضُد and so was lightened; and the same holds for it with the fāʾ and the lām, as in فهو and لهو. It is [also] read with ḍamma, according to the original form.

ukberi-tibyan:30-30.t:
Allah the Exalted says: (وَإِذْ قَالَ رَبُّكَ لِلْمَلَائِكَةِ إِنِّي جَاعِلٌ فِي الْأَرْضِ خَلِيفَةً قَالُوا أَتَجْعَلُ فِيهَا مَنْ يُفْسِدُ فِيهَا وَيَسْفِكُ الدِّمَاءَ وَنَحْنُ نُسَبِّحُ بِحَمْدِكَ وَنُقَدِّسُ لَكَ قَالَ إِنِّي أَعْلَمُ مَا لَا تَعْلَمُونَ (٣٠)).
His saying, Exalted is He: (وَإِذْ قَالَ): it is a mafʿūl bihi (direct object), its implied form being: "and remember when [your Lord] said".
It has also been said: it is the khabar (predicate) of an omitted mubtadaʾ (subject), its implied form being: "and the beginning of My creation was when your Lord said". It has also been said: it is redundant (zāʾida). And (لِلْمَلَائِكَةِ): there is disagreement about its singular and its origin. Some said that its singular was originally مألك on the pattern مفعل, because it is derived from الألوكة, which is "message"; from this is the poet's saying:
وَغُلَامٍ أَرْسَلَتْهُ أُمُّهُ بِأَلُوكَ فَبَذَلْنَا مَا سَأَلْ.
(And many a lad whose mother sent him with a message, so we gave what he asked.)
So the hamza is the first radical (fāʾ) of the word; then it was moved back and placed after the lām, and they said ملأك; the poet said:
فَلَسْتُ لِإِنْسِيٍّ وَلَكِنْ لِمَلَاكٍ تَنَزَّلَ ... مِنْ جَوِّ السَّمَاءِ يَصُوبُ.
(For I am not [kin] to a human, but to an angel who descended from the vault of the sky, swooping down.)
So its pattern now is معفل, and the plural is ملائكة on the pattern معافلة.
Others said: the root of the word is لأك, so the second radical (ʿayn) of the word is a hamza, and the origin of ملك is ملأك without any transposition. On both views the vowel of the hamza was cast onto the lām and the hamza was omitted; then when it was put in the plural it was restored, so its pattern now is مفاعلة.
Others said: the second radical of the word is wāw, and it is from لاك يلوك, said when one turns something over in one's mouth; as if the bearer of the message turns it over in his mouth. So the origin of ملك would be like معاد, then its second radical was omitted for lightness, and the origin of ملائكة would be like مقاولة; then the wāw was changed to hamza, as the wāw of مصائب was changed.
Others said: ملك is فعل from المُلك, which is strength; so the mīm is a radical and there is no omission in it, but it was given the plural on the pattern فعائلة irregularly (shādhdh). (جَاعِلٌ): the future is intended by it, and for that reason it governs.
It may be in the sense of خالق ("creating"), and so take one object, or in the sense of مصيّر ("making into"), and so take two objects, in which case في الأرض is the second. (خَلِيفَةً): فعيلة in the sense of فاعل, i.e. one who succeeds another; the hāʾ was added for intensiveness.
(أَتَجْعَلُ): the hamza is for seeking guidance, i.e. "will You place therein one who will cause corruption, as there was in it before?"
It has also been said: they were asking about their own states, i.e. "will You place therein one who causes corruption while we remain in obedience to You, or will we change?" (يَسْفِكُ): the majority read it without doubling and with kasra on the fāʾ; it has also been read with ḍamma on it, and both are dialectal variants; and it is read with doubling (tashdīd) for multiplicity. The hamza of (الدِّمَاءَ) is converted from a yāʾ, because the original form is دمى, since they said دميان.
(بِحَمْدِكَ): in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial), its implied form being: "we glorify [You], encompassed by Your praise", or "worshipping by Your praise". (وَنُقَدِّسُ لَكَ): i.e. "for Your sake"; the lām may also be redundant, i.e. "we sanctify You".
It may also be a lām that makes the verb transitive, like the transitivizing bāʾ, as in سجدت لله ("I prostrated to Allah").
(إِنِّي أَعْلَمُ): the original form is إنّني; the middle nūn was omitted, not the nūn of protection (nūn al-wiqāya); this is the correct view. (وَأَعْلَمُ): it may be a verb, with ما as its object, either in the sense of الذي or as an indefinite noun qualified by an adjective, the referring pronoun being omitted. It may also be a noun like أفضل, in which case ما is in the position of the genitive by iḍāfa.
It may also be in the position of the accusative by أعلم, as in their saying: هؤلاء حواجُّ بيتَ الله ("these are pilgrims to the House of Allah"), with the accusative and the genitive; and the tanwīn is dropped because this noun is a diptote. If you say: "أفعل does not take an object in the accusative", it is answered: if من is intended along with it, it does not; but أعلم here is in the sense of عالم ("knowing"). It may also be that by أعلم is meant "more knowing than you", in which case «ما» is in the position of the accusative by an omitted verb indicated by the noun; and similar to it is His saying: (هُوَ أَعْلَمُ مَنْ يَضِلُّ عَنْ سَبِيلِهِ).

ukberi-tibyan:72-72.t:
Allah the Exalted said: (وَإِذْ قَتَلْتُمْ نَفْسًا فَادَّارَأْتُمْ فِيهَا وَاللَّهُ مُخْرِجٌ مَا كُنْتُمْ تَكْتُمُونَ (٧٢)).
(وَإِذْ قَتَلْتُمْ): its implied form is "remember when (اذْكُرُوا إِذْ)".
(فَادَّارَأْتُمْ): the original form of the word is تَدَارَأْتُمْ, and its pattern is تَفَاعَلْتُمْ. Then they wanted to lighten it, so they changed the tāʾ into a dāl, so that it would be of the same kind as the dāl which is the first radical (fāʾ) of the word, to make assimilation (idghām) possible. Then they made the dāl quiescent, since the condition of assimilation is that the first letter be quiescent; and since it was not possible to begin with a quiescent letter, a connecting hamza (hamzat al-waṣl) was brought in for it. So its pattern now is افَّاعَلْتُمْ with a doubled fāʾ, transformed from اتْفَاعَلْتُمْ. The first fāʾ is redundant (zāʾida), but it has become of the same kind as the radical, so it is pronounced doubled — not because both are radicals, but because the added letter is of the same kind as the radical. So it is
parallel to your saying ضَرَّبَ with the doubling: one of the two rāʾs is added, and its pattern is فَعَّلَ with a doubled ʿayn, just as the rāʾ is so. We did not say in the pattern فَعْرَلَ or فَرْعَلَ, bringing the added rāʾ into the model; rather the ʿayn was added in the model just as it was added in the original, and it was of the same kind as it. Likewise the tāʾ in تَدَارَأْتُمْ became, by substitution, a dāl of the same kind as the first radical of the word.
If one asks about the pattern in order to distinguish the radical from the added letter, by its first or its second form, the answer is to say: the pattern of its first original form is تَفَاعَلْتُمْ; of the second, اتْفَاعَلْتُمْ; and of the third, افَّاعَلْتُمْ. Like this case is: (اثَّاقَلْتُمْ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ), and (حَتَّى إِذَا ادَّارَكُوا فِيهَا).
His saying, the Exalted: (مُخْرِجٌ مَا كُنْتُمْ تَكْتُمُونَ): ((مَا)) is in the position of the accusative, governed by مُخْرِجٌ. It means "that which" (al-ladhī), and the returning pronoun (al-ʿāʾid) is omitted. It may also be maṣdariyya (forming a verbal noun), the maṣdar (verbal noun) then having the sense of the passive participle; i.e. "He brings out your concealing", i.e. "what you conceal".

ukberi-tibyan:73-73.t:
Allah the Exalted said: (فَقُلْنَا اضْرِبُوهُ بِبَعْضِهَا كَذَلِكَ يُحْيِي اللَّهُ الْمَوْتَى وَيُرِيكُمْ آيَاتِهِ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَعْقِلُونَ (٧٣)).
His saying, the Exalted: (كَذَلِكَ يُحْيِي اللَّهُ): the kāf is in the position of the accusative as a naʿt (adjective) of an omitted maṣdar (verbal noun), its implied form being: "Allah gives life to the dead with a giving of life like that". And in the speech there is an omission, its implied form being: "so they struck it, and it came to life".

ukberi-tibyan:74-74.t:
Allah the Exalted said: (ثُمَّ قَسَتْ قُلُوبُكُمْ مِنْ بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ فَهِيَ كَالْحِجَارَةِ أَوْ أَشَدُّ قَسْوَةً وَإِنَّ مِنَ الْحِجَارَةِ لَمَا يَتَفَجَّرُ مِنْهُ الْأَنْهَارُ وَإِنَّ مِنْهَا لَمَا يَشَّقَّقُ فَيَخْرُجُ مِنْهُ الْمَاءُ وَإِنَّ مِنْهَا لَمَا يَهْبِطُ مِنْ خَشْيَةِ اللَّهِ وَمَا اللَّهُ بِغَافِلٍ عَمَّا تَعْمَلُونَ (٧٤)).
His saying, the Exalted: (فَهِيَ كَالْحِجَارَةِ): the kāf is a preposition attached (mutaʿalliq) to something omitted, its implied form being: "so they are settled (مُسْتَقِرَّةٌ) like the stones". It may also be a noun meaning "like" (مِثْل), in the position of the nominative, and then it is not attached to anything.
(أَوْ أَشَدُّ): «أَوْ» here is like أَوْ in His saying: (أَوْ كَصَيِّبٍ). And أَشَدُّ is maʿṭūf (conjoined) to the kāf, its implied form being: "or they are harder". It was also read with a fatḥa on the dāl, as being genitive by conjunction with الْحِجَارَةِ, its implied form being: "or like what is harder than the stones". And (قَسْوَةً): a tamyīz (specification), and it is a maṣdar (verbal noun). (لَمَا يَتَفَجَّرُ): مَا means "that which", in the position of the accusative as the noun of إِنَّ, and the lām is for emphasis.
Had it been read with the tāʾ [i.e. تَتَفَجَّرُ], it would be permissible; and were it outside the Quran, «مِنْهَا» would be permissible, according to the sense. (يَشَّقَّقُ): its original form is يَتَشَقَّقُ; the tāʾ was changed into a shīn and assimilated. Its fāʿil (agent) is the pronoun of مَا.
Its fāʿil may also be the pronoun of الْمَاءُ, because يَشَقَّقُ may be assigned to the water according to the sense; so you have two verbs, and the second of them governs الْمَاءُ, while the fāʿil of the first is concealed on condition of its being explained [by what follows]. According to the Kufans, the first governs, so that in the second there is its pronoun.
(مِنْ خَشْيَةِ اللَّهِ): مِنْ is in the position of the accusative, governed by (يَهْبِطُ), just as you say: "it descends through fear of Allah (يَهْبِطُ بِخَشْيَةِ اللَّهِ)".
(عَمَّا تَعْمَلُونَ): مَا means "that which", and it may also be maṣdariyya (forming a verbal noun).

ukberi-tibyan:75-75.t:
Allah the Exalted said: (أَفَتَطْمَعُونَ أَنْ يُؤْمِنُوا لَكُمْ وَقَدْ كَانَ فَرِيقٌ مِنْهُمْ يَسْمَعُونَ كَلَامَ اللَّهِ ثُمَّ يُحَرِّفُونَهُ مِنْ بَعْدِ مَا عَقَلُوهُ وَهُمْ يَعْلَمُونَ (٧٥)).
His saying, the Exalted: (أَنْ يُؤْمِنُوا لَكُمْ): the preposition is omitted, i.e. "in that they should believe (فِي أَنْ يُؤْمِنُوا)"; and mention has already been made of the grammatical position of the like of this. (وَقَدْ كَانَ): the wāw is the wāw of the ḥāl (circumstantial), and the implied meaning is: "Do you then hope for their belief, when their way is lying and distortion?" مِنْهُمْ is in the position of the nominative as an adjective of فَرِيقٌ, and يَسْمَعُونَ is the khabar (predicate) of كَانَ. Some allowed يَسْمَعُونَ to be an adjective of فَرِيقٌ and مِنْهُمْ to be the khabar, but that is weak. (مَا عَقَلُوهُ): مَا is maṣdariyya (forming a verbal noun). وَهُمْ يَعْلَمُونَ is a ḥāl, and what governs it is يُحَرِّفُونَهُ; it may also be that what governs it is عَقَلُوهُ, and then it is a corroborative ḥāl (ḥāl muʾakkida).

ukberi-tibyan:76-76.t:
Allah the Exalted said: (وَإِذَا خَلَا بَعْضُهُمْ إِلَى بَعْضٍ قَالُوا أَتُحَدِّثُونَهُمْ بِمَا فَتَحَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْكُمْ لِيُحَاجُّوكُمْ بِهِ عِنْدَ رَبِّكُمْ أَفَلَا تَعْقِلُونَ (٧٦)).
His saying, the Exalted: (بِمَا فَتَحَ اللَّهُ): مَا may mean "that which", may be maṣdariyya (forming a verbal noun), and may be an indefinite noun qualified by an adjective (nakira mawṣūfa). (لِيُحَاجُّوكُمْ): the lām has the sense of كَيْ ("so that"), and what puts the verb in the accusative is a concealed أَنْ, because the lām is in reality a preposition and enters only on a noun. Most of the Arabs give this lām a kasra, and some of them give it a fatḥa.

ukberi-tibyan:31-31.t:
Allah the Exalted says: (وَعَلَّمَ آدَمَ الْأَسْمَاءَ كُلَّهَا ثُمَّ عَرَضَهُمْ عَلَى الْمَلَائِكَةِ فَقَالَ أَنْبِئُونِي بِأَسْمَاءِ هَؤُلَاءِ إِنْ كُنْتُمْ صَادِقِينَ (٣١)).
His saying, Exalted is He: (وَعَلَّمَ): it may be resumptive, or conjoined to (قَالَ رَبُّكَ), and [then] in the position of the genitive, like the position of قال; this is strengthened by the agent being implied. It has been read «وَعُلِّمَ آدَمُ», as a verb whose agent is not named (passive). And (آدَمَ) is أفعل, and the alif in it replaces a hamza which is the first radical (fāʾ) of the word, because it is derived from أديم الأرض ("the surface of the earth") or from الأُدمة ("brown complexion"). Its pattern cannot be فاعل, since if it were so it would be fully declinable, like عالم and خاتم; definiteness alone does not prevent declension, and it is not a foreign word.
(ثُمَّ عَرَضَهُمْ): meaning the bearers of the names; for that reason the pronoun is masculine.
(هَؤُلَاءِ إِنْ كُنْتُمْ): it is read with full pronunciation (taḥqīq) of both hamzas, according to the original form. It is also read with a single hamza; it has been said that the omitted one is the first, because it is the last radical (lām) of the word, while the other is the beginning of the next word, and omitting the final one is more appropriate.
It has also been said that the omitted one is the second, because the heaviness arose with it.
It is also read with softening (talyīn) of the first hamza and full pronunciation of the second, and the reverse; and some of them change the second into a quiescent yāʾ, as if he regarded the two as being in a single word, seeking lightness.

ukberi-tibyan:32-32.t:
Allah the Exalted says: (قَالُوا سُبْحَانَكَ لَا عِلْمَ لَنَا إِلَّا مَا عَلَّمْتَنَا إِنَّكَ أَنْتَ الْعَلِيمُ الْحَكِيمُ (٣٢)).
His saying, Exalted is He: (سُبْحَانَكَ): سبحان is a noun occupying the place of the maṣdar (verbal noun); from it سبّحتُ and التسبيح were derived. It is hardly ever used except as a muḍāf, because the iḍāfa makes clear who is being glorified. When it is detached from the iḍāfa it is a proper name (ʿalam) for glorification, a diptote because of definiteness and the alif and nūn at its end, like عثمان. It has occurred in poetry with tanwīn, in the manner of the tanwīn of a proper name when it is made indefinite. What it is annexed to is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object), because it is the one glorified.
It may also be the agent, because the meaning is "You are exalted above [all imperfection]". It is accusative as a maṣdar by an omitted verb, its implied form being: سبّحتُ الله تسبيحا ("I glorify Allah with glorification").
(إِلَّا مَا عَلَّمْتَنَا): ما is maṣdariyya (forming a maṣdar), i.e. "except a knowledge You have taught us"; its position is nominative as a badal (substitute) from the position of لا علم, as in your saying: لا إلهَ إلا اللهُ.
It may also be that ما is in the sense of الذي, with علم in the sense of معلوم ("what is known"), i.e. "nothing known to us except what You have taught us". It is not permissible for ما to be in the position of the accusative by العلم, because the noun of لا, when it governs what comes after it, is not made indeclinable. (إِنَّكَ أَنْتَ الْعَلِيمُ): أنت is a mubtadaʾ (subject) and العليم is its khabar (predicate), and the clause is the khabar of إنّ.
It may also be that أنت is a tawkīd (emphasis) of the accusative pronoun; it occurs in the form of the nominative because it is, in meaning, the kāf itself. إياك does not occur here for emphasis, because if it occurred it would be a badal, and إياك is not used for emphasis.
It may also be a separating pronoun (faṣl) having no grammatical position.
And (الْحَكِيمُ): a second khabar, or a ṣifa (adjective) of العليم according to the view of those who allow an adjective of an adjective; and that is correct, because this adjective is in meaning the thing described.
العليم is in the sense of العالم ("knowing"). As for الحكيم, it may be in the sense of الحاكم ("judging"), or in the sense of المُحكِم ("making precise").

ukberi-tibyan:33-33.t:
Allah the Exalted says: (قَالَ يَا آدَمُ أَنْبِئْهُمْ بِأَسْمَائِهِمْ فَلَمَّا أَنْبَأَهُمْ بِأَسْمَائِهِمْ قَالَ أَلَمْ أَقُلْ لَكُمْ إِنِّي أَعْلَمُ غَيْبَ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَأَعْلَمُ مَا تُبْدُونَ وَمَا كُنْتُمْ تَكْتُمُونَ (٣٣)).
His saying, Exalted is He: (أَنْبِئْهُمْ): it is read with full pronunciation of the hamza, according to the original form, and with yāʾ by softening the hamza; he did not change it by a regular (qiyāsī) change, because if it were so, the yāʾ would be omitted, as it is omitted in your saying أبقِهم, from بقيتُ.
It has also been read أنبِهم, with kasra on the bāʾ, without hamza or yāʾ, on the basis that the change of the hamza into yāʾ is a regular change.
أنبأ is transitive by itself to one object, and to the second by a preposition, namely His saying: بأسمائهم; it may also be made transitive by عن, as in your saying: أنبأته عن حال زيد ("I informed him about Zayd's condition"). As for His saying, Exalted is He: (قَدْ نَبَّأَنَا اللَّهُ مِنْ), it will be mentioned in its place.
(وَأَعْلَمُ مَا تُبْدُونَ): resumptive, and not reported speech governed by His saying: ألم أقل لكم; it may also be reported speech, in which case it is in the position of the accusative. The pattern of تبدون is تُفعون, and what is omitted from it is its last radical (lām), which is a wāw, because it is from بدا يبدو.
The original state of the yāʾ in إنّي is to be vowelled with fatḥa, because it is a pronoun consisting of a single letter, so it is vowelled like the kāf in إنّك. Whoever vowels it brings it out according to the original form, and whoever makes it quiescent finds the vowel on the yāʾ after a kasra heavy.

ukberi-tibyan:34-34.t:
Allah the Exalted says: (وَإِذْ قُلْنَا لِلْمَلَائِكَةِ اسْجُدُوا لِآدَمَ فَسَجَدُوا إِلَّا إِبْلِيسَ أَبَى وَاسْتَكْبَرَ وَكَانَ مِنَ الْكَافِرِينَ (٣٤)).
His saying, Exalted is He: (لِلْمَلَائِكَةِ اسْجُدُوا): the majority read it with kasra on the tāʾ.
It has been read with ḍamma on it, and this is a very weak reading. The best way to account for it is that the transmitter did not record the reciter accurately: the reciter pointed towards the ḍamma (ishāra) to indicate that the omitted hamza is pronounced with ḍamma when starting, and the transmitter did not perceive this indication.
It has also been said that he intended a pause on the tāʾ as quiescent, then vowelled it with ḍamma to harmonize with the ḍamma of the jīm; this is treating continuous speech as if it were a pause. Similar to it is what is reported of a woman who saw some women with a man among them, and said: أفي السَّوَ تَنْتُنَّه ("Is it in evil that you are [engaged]?"), with fatḥa on the tāʾ; it is as if she intended a pause on the tāʾ, then cast onto it the vowel of the hamza, and it became vowelled with fatḥa.
(إِلَّا إِبْلِيسَ): a disjoined exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ), because he was not one of the angels. It has also been said that it is a joined (muttaṣil) exception, because he was originally an angel. It is a foreign noun, a diptote because of foreignness and definiteness.
It has also been said: it is Arabic, derived from الإبلاس ("despair"), and it is a diptote because of definiteness and because it has no parallel among nouns; but this is far-fetched, and besides there are nouns like it, such as إخريط, إجفيل, إصليت and the like. (وَأَبَى): in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial) from إبليس; its implied form is: "he abandoned the prostration, averse to it and arrogant".
(وَكَانَ مِنَ الْكَافِرِينَ): resumptive; it may also be in the position of a ḥāl.

ukberi-tibyan:35-35.t:
Allah the Exalted says: (وَقُلْنَا يَا آدَمُ اسْكُنْ أَنْتَ وَزَوْجُكَ الْجَنَّةَ وَكُلَا مِنْهَا رَغَدًا حَيْثُ شِئْتُمَا وَلَا تَقْرَبَا هَذِهِ الشَّجَرَةَ فَتَكُونَا مِنَ الظَّالِمِينَ) ((٣٥)).
His saying, Exalted is He: (اسْكُنْ أَنْتَ وَزَوْجُكَ): أنت is a tawkīd (emphasis) of the pronoun in the verb, brought so that conjunction onto it is valid. The original form of كُل is أُؤكُل, like اقتُل, except that the Arabs omitted the second hamza for lightness; similar to it is خُذ, and it is not taken as a model for analogy, so you do not say جُر as the imperative of أجَر يأجُر. Sībawayh reported أُوكُل as irregular (shādhdh). (مِنْهَا): i.e. "from its fruit"; the muḍāf was omitted. Its position is accusative by the verb before it, and من is for the beginning of the extent.
And (رَغَدًا): an adjective of an omitted maṣdar, i.e. "an abundant eating", i.e. pleasant and wholesome.
It may also be a maṣdar in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial), its implied form being: "eat, the two of you, finding it pleasant and wholesome".
(حَيْثُ): an adverbial of place, its operator being كلا. It may also be a badal (substitute) from الجنة, in which case حيث is a mafʿūl bihi (direct object), because الجنة is an object and not an adverbial (ẓarf), since you say سكنت البصرة ("I dwelt in Basra") and سكنت الدار ("I dwelt in the house") in the sense of "I settled in"; so it is like your saying: "settle in the house wherever you wish". (هَذِهِ الشَّجَرَةَ): the hāʾ replaces the yāʾ in هذي, because for the feminine you say هذي, هاتا and هاتي; the yāʾ marks the feminine with the dhāl and nothing else, and the hāʾ replaces it because it resembles it in faintness. الشجرة is a naʿt (adjective) of هذه. In an irregular reading it was read «هذه الشِّيَرة», which is a dialect in which the jīm was changed to yāʾ because of its closeness to it in point of articulation.
(فَتَكُونَا): the answer to the prohibition, because the implied form is: "if you approach, you will be"; the omission of the nūn here is the sign of the accusative: the answer to a prohibition, when it is with the fāʾ, is accusative. It may also be jussive by conjunction.

ukberi-tibyan:36-36.t:
Allah the Exalted says: (فَأَزَلَّهُمَا الشَّيْطَانُ عَنْهَا فَأَخْرَجَهُمَا مِمَّا كَانَا فِيهِ وَقُلْنَا اهْبِطُوا بَعْضُكُمْ لِبَعْضٍ عَدُوٌّ وَلَكُمْ فِي الْأَرْضِ مُسْتَقَرٌّ وَمَتَاعٌ إِلَى حِينٍ (٣٦)).
His saying, Exalted is He: (فَأَزَلَّهُمَا): it is read with doubling of the lām and without alif, i.e. "he led them both into a slip"; and it is read فأزالهما, i.e. "he removed them both", which is from your saying: زال الشيء يزول, when a thing leaves its place, and أزلتُه, "I removed it"; its alif is converted from a wāw.
(مِمَّا كَانَا فِيهِ): ما is in the sense of الذي; it may also be an indefinite noun qualified by an adjective, i.e. "from a bliss" or "a life". اهبطوا: the majority read it with kasra on the bāʾ, which is the most eloquent dialect; it has been read with ḍamma on it, which is a dialectal variant. (بَعْضُكُمْ لِبَعْضٍ عَدُوٌّ): a clause in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the wāw in اهبطوا, i.e. "go down, being enemies to one another". The lām is attached to عدوّ, because the implied form is بعضكم عدوّ لبعض, and عدوّ operates like a verb, but by way of the preposition. It may also be an adjective of عدوّ; then, when it was placed before it, it became a ḥāl.
The clause may also be resumptive. As for عدوّ being singular, it may be that since بعضكم is singular in form, عدوّ was made singular; and it may be that the singular was put in place of the plural, as He said: (فَإِنَّهُمْ عَدُوٌّ لِي).
(وَلَكُمْ فِي الْأَرْضِ مُسْتَقَرٌّ): it may be resumptive, and it may also be a ḥāl, its implied form being: "go down, being enemies to one another and deserving of a dwelling".
And (مُسْتَقَرٌّ) may be a maṣdar in the sense of الاستقرار ("dwelling"), and it may be the place of dwelling. And (إِلَى حِينٍ) may be in the position of the nominative as an adjective of متاع, and so be attached to something omitted; and it may be in the position of the accusative by متاع, because it has the status of a maṣdar, the implied form being: "and that you enjoy yourselves until a time".

ukberi-tibyan:37-37.t:
Allah the Exalted says: (فَتَلَقَّى آدَمُ مِنْ رَبِّهِ كَلِمَاتٍ فَتَابَ عَلَيْهِ إِنَّهُ هُوَ التَّوَّابُ الرَّحِيمُ (٣٧)).
His saying, Exalted is He: (فَتَلَقَّى آدَمُ): it is read with آدم in the nominative and كلمات in the accusative, and the reverse, because whatever meets you, you have met it. And (مِنْ رَبِّهِ) may be in the position of the accusative by تلقى, being for the beginning of the extent.
It may also be in the position of the accusative as an adjective of كلمات, its implied form being: "words coming from his Lord"; then when it was placed before it, it became accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial).
(إِنَّهُ هُوَ التَّوَّابُ): هو here is like أنت in (إِنَّكَ أَنْتَ الْعَلِيمُ الْحَكِيمُ), and that has been mentioned.

ukberi-tibyan:1-1.t:
His saying, the Exalted: (الم (١)). Each one of these disjointed letters (al-ḥurūf al-muqaṭṭaʿa) is a noun. Alif is a noun used to express a letter like the one in قَالَ; lām is used to express the last letter of قَالَ; and likewise whatever resembles them. The proof that they are nouns is that each of them indicates a meaning in itself. They are indeclinable (mabnī), because you do not intend to predicate anything of them; they merely reproduce the sounds of the letters for which they were made names. So they are like sound-words, such as غَاقٍ in imitating the cry of the crow.
There are three views on the grammatical position of (الم). First: the genitive, as an oath; the particle of the oath is omitted, and its governing effect remains after the omission, because it is intended and so is like something pronounced, just as they said اللَّهِ لَتَفْعَلَنَّ ("By Allah, you shall surely do it") in the dialect of those who use the genitive. Second: its position is accusative, and there are two views on this. One: it is on the assumption that the oath [particle] is omitted, as you say اللَّهَ لَأَفْعَلَنَّ, and what puts it in the accusative is an omitted verb, its implied form being "I bind myself to Allah", i.e. to the oath by Him. The other: it is a mafʿūl bihi (direct object), its implied form being "Recite الم". The third view: its position is nominative, as a mubtadaʾ (subject), with what follows it as the khabar (predicate).

ukberi-tibyan:2-2.t:
Allah the Exalted said: (ذَلِكَ الْكِتَابُ لَا رَيْبَ فِيهِ هُدًى لِلْمُتَّقِينَ (٢)).
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: (ذَلِكَ): ذَا is a demonstrative, and the alif is part of the noun.
The Kufans said: the dhāl alone is the noun, and the alif was added to increase the size of the word. They took as evidence for this their saying ذِهِ أَمَةُ اللَّهِ ("this is the handmaid of Allah"). That amounts to nothing, because this noun is an overt noun, and in the language there is no overt noun consisting of a single letter on which this could be modelled. What shows this is their saying in the diminutive ذَيًّا, returning it to a three-letter form. The hāʾ in ذِهِ is a substitute for the yāʾ in ذِي.
As for the lām, it is a particle added to indicate the remoteness of what is pointed to.
It is also said that it is a substitute for هَا: do you not see that you say هَذَا and هَذَاكَ, but هَذَلِكَ is not permitted?
The lām was given a vowel so that two quiescent letters would not meet, and it was given kasra according to the basic rule for the meeting of two quiescent letters. It is also said that it was given kasra to distinguish this lām from the lām of the genitive, since if you gave it fatḥa and said ذَلِكَ [Translator's note: so in the text; the intended form is evidently ذَا لَكَ / ذَلَكَ, with fatḥa on the lām], it would be confused with the meaning of possession.
It is also said that ذَلِكَ here has the meaning of هَذَا. Its position is nominative: either as the khabar (predicate) of الم, with الْكِتَابُ as ʿaṭf bayān (explicative apposition) and لَا رَيْبَ in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial), i.e. "this is the Book, truly", or "not subject to doubt"; or ذَلِكَ is a mubtadaʾ (subject), الْكِتَابُ its khabar, and لَا رَيْبَ a ḥāl. It is also possible that الْكِتَابُ is ʿaṭf bayān and لَا رَيْبَ فِيهِ the khabar. رَيْبَ is indeclinable (mabnī) according to most, because it has been compounded with لَا and made like خَمْسَةَ عَشَرَ. The reason for its being indeclinable is that it implicitly contains the meaning of مِنْ, since the implied wording is "there is not any doubt" (لَا مِنْ رَيْبٍ); and مِنْ needed to be implied so that لَا would indicate the negation of the whole genus. Do you not see that you say لَا رَجُلَ فِي الدَّارِ ("there is no man in the house"), negating one and more than one; but if you say لَا رَجُلٌ فِي الدَّارِ, in the nominative with nunation, you negate one and do not negate more than one, since there could be two or more in it.
His saying (فِيهِ): there are two views on it. First: it is in the position of the khabar of لَا and is attached (mutaʿalliq) to something omitted, its implied form being "no doubt is existing in it"; in that case one pauses on فِيهِ. The second view: لَا رَيْبَ is the end of the statement and its khabar is omitted because it is known; then you begin anew and say فِيهِ هُدًى, so that هُدًى is a mubtadaʾ and فِيهِ the khabar; or, if you wish, هُدًى is a fāʿil (agent) put in the nominative by فِيهِ. On both views فِي is attached to an omitted verb.
As for هُدًى, its alif is converted from a yāʾ, because you say هَدَيْتُ and الْهُدَى.
There are two views on its position. First: nominative — either as a mubtadaʾ or as a fāʿil, as we mentioned; or as the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, i.e. "it is guidance"; or as a khabar of ذَلِكَ after another khabar.
The second view: it is in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl from the hāʾ in فِيهِ, i.e. "there is no doubt in it, as a guide". The maṣdar (verbal noun) here has the meaning of the active participle, and what governs the ḥāl is the meaning of the clause, its implied form being "I affirm it as a guide". It is also possible that what governs it is the meaning of drawing attention and pointing produced by His saying ذَلِكَ.
His saying, the Exalted: (لِلْمُتَّقِينَ): the lām is attached to something omitted, its implied form being كَائِنٌ ("being") or كَائِنًا, according to the two views we mentioned on هُدًى. It is also possible for the lām to be attached to هُدًى itself, because it is a maṣdar, and the maṣdar governs as the verb does. The singular of الْمُتَّقِينَ is مُتَّقِي. The root of the word is وَقَى, on the pattern faʿala; its first radical is wāw and its last radical is yāʾ. When you form iftaʿala from it, you turn the wāw into tāʾ and assimilate it into the other tāʾ, saying اتَّقَى; and likewise in the active participle and its other derived forms, such as مُتَّقٍ and مُتَّقًى.
مُتَّقٍ is a defective noun (ism nāqiṣ); its yāʾ, which is the final radical, is dropped in the plural because it is quiescent and the letter of the plural after it is quiescent, as in your saying مُتَّقُونَ and مُتَّقِينَ. Its pattern originally is muftaʿilūn, because its original form is مُوْتَقِيُونَ; then the final radical was dropped for the reason we mentioned, so that its pattern now is muftaʿūn and muftaʿīn. The final radical was dropped rather than the sign of the plural only because the sign of the plural indicates a meaning, and if it were dropped no indication of that meaning would remain; so keeping it was more appropriate.

ukberi-tibyan:126-126.t:
Allah the Exalted said: {وَإِذ قَالَ إِبْرَاهِيم رب اجْعَل هَذَا بَلَدا آمنا وارزق أَهله من الثمرات من آمن مِنْهُم بِاللَّه وَالْيَوْم الآخر قَالَ وَمن كفر فأمتعه قَلِيلا ثمَّ أضطره إِلَى عَذَاب النَّار وَبئسَ الْمصير}
His saying, Exalted is He: (اجْعَلْ هَذَا بَلَدًا): اجْعَلْ means "make into" (صَيِّرْ); هَذَا is the first object, بَلَدًا is the second object, and (آمِنًا) is an adjective (ṣifa) of the second object. As for the one in [Sūrat] Ibrāhīm, it will be mentioned there.
(مَنْ آمَنَ): مَنْ is a badal (substitute) for أَهْلَهُ, and it is a substitution of part for whole. (وَمَنْ كَفَرَ): there are two views on مَنْ. The first: it means "the one who" (الَّذِي) or is an indefinite noun qualified by an adjective, and its position is accusative; the implied form is: "He said: and I will provide for whoever disbelieves" (وَأَرْزُقُ مَنْ كَفَرَ), and the verb was omitted because the context indicates it.
(فَأُمَتِّعُهُ): conjoined to the omitted verb. On this view it is not permissible for مَنْ to be a mubtadaʾ (subject) with «فَأُمَتِّعُهُ» as its khabar (predicate), because the fāʾ does not enter the khabar of الَّذِي unless the khabar is merited by its ṣila (relative clause), as when you say: الَّذِي يَأْتِينِي فَلَهُ دِرْهَمٌ ("whoever comes to me gets a dirham"); and disbelief does not merit being granted enjoyment. If you make the fāʾ redundant (zāʾida), according to the view of al-Akhfash, it is permissible; and if you make the khabar omitted, with «فَأُمَتِّعُهُ» as an indication of it, it is permissible, its implied form being: "and whoever disbelieves, I will provide for him, and so I will give him enjoyment" (وَمَنْ كَفَرَ أَرْزُقُهُ فَأُمَتِّعُهُ). The second view: that «مَنْ» is conditional, and the fāʾ [introduces] its apodosis (jawāb); and it is said that the apodosis is omitted, its implied form being: "and whoever disbelieves, I will provide for him". On this view مَنْ is nominative as a mubtadaʾ, and it may not be accusative, because a conditional particle is not governed by its apodosis, but rather by the protasis (al-sharṭ). On both views كَفَرَ means يَكْفُرُ ("disbelieves"). The well-known reading is فَأُمَتِّعُهُ with doubling [of the tāʾ] and ḍamma on the final radical (ʿayn) [i.e. the ʿayn of أُمَتِّعُ], for the reason we mentioned: that it is either conjoined or a khabar.
It was read, as an irregular (shādhdh) reading, with sukūn on the ʿayn, and there are two views about it. The first: that the vowel was dropped for lightness because of the succession of vowels.
The second: that the fāʾ is redundant and أُمَتِّعُهُ is the apodosis of the condition. It is also read with the tāʾ undoubled, both with ḍamma on the ʿayn and with sukūn, according to what we have mentioned. And it is read فَأُمَتِّعُهُ in the form of the imperative, and on this reading it is part of what is reported from Ibrāhīm.
(قَلِيلًا): an adjective (naʿt) of an omitted maṣdar (verbal noun), or of an omitted adverb of time.
(ثُمَّ أَضْطَرُّهُ): the majority read it with the rāʾ nominative, and it was read with fatḥa on it and a connecting hamza, as an imperative, as stated before. (وَبِئْسَ الْمَصِيرُ): الْمَصِيرُ is the fāʾil (agent) of بِئْسَ, and the one specifically singled out for blame (al-makhṣūṣ bi-l-dhamm) is omitted, its implied form being: "and evil is the destination — the Fire" (وَبِئْسَ الْمَصِيرُ النَّارُ).

ukberi-tibyan:127-127.t:
Allah the Exalted said: (وَإِذْ يَرْفَعُ إِبْرَاهِيمُ الْقَوَاعِدَ مِنَ الْبَيْتِ وَإِسْمَاعِيلُ رَبَّنَا تَقَبَّلْ مِنَّا. . . . . . (١٢٧)).
His saying, Exalted is He: (مِنَ الْبَيْتِ): in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial) from الْقَوَاعِدَ, i.e. "being part of the House"; and it may be in the position of the accusative as a mafʿūl bihi (direct object), in the sense that he raised them up from the ground of the House.
And (الْقَوَاعِدَ): the plural of قَاعِدَةٌ ("foundation"); whereas the singular of قَوَاعِدُ النِّسَاءِ ("women past childbearing") is قَاعِدٌ. (وَإِسْمَاعِيلُ): conjoined to إِبْرَاهِيمُ, and the implied form is: "both saying: our Lord", and "both saying" is in the position of a ḥāl. It is also said that إِسْمَاعِيلُ is a mubtadaʾ (subject) whose khabar (predicate) is omitted, its implied form being: "says: our Lord", because the builder was Ibrāhīm and the one making supplication was Ismāʿīl.

ukberi-tibyan:128-128.t:
Allah the Exalted said: (رَبَّنَا وَاجْعَلْنَا مُسْلِمَيْنِ لَكَ وَمِنْ ذُرِّيَّتِنَا أُمَّةً مُسْلِمَةً لَكَ وَأَرِنَا مَنَاسِكَنَا. . . . . . . . (١٢٨)).
His saying, Exalted is He: (مُسْلِمَيْنِ لَكَ): a second object; and (لَكَ) is attached (mutaʿalliq) to مُسْلِمَيْنِ, because it means "we submit to You", i.e. "we devote ourselves sincerely"; and it may be an adjective (naʿt), i.e. "submitting, acting for You". (وَمِنْ ذُرِّيَّتِنَا): مِنْ may be for the beginning of the extent of the "making", so it would be a second object.
And (أُمَّةً) is a first object, and (مُسْلِمَةً) is an adjective of أُمَّةً, and «لَكَ» is as stated before regarding مُسْلِمَيْنِ. It is also possible for «أُمَّةً» to be the first object and «وَمِنْ ذُرِّيَّتِنَا» an adjective of أُمَّةً that was placed before it and so became accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial), with مُسْلِمَةً as the second object. The wāw originally enters upon أُمَّةً, and it has been separated from it by His saying (وَمِنْ ذُرِّيَّتِنَا); this is permissible because it is part of the conjoined speech. (وَأَرِنَا): the original form is أَرْئِنَا; the hamza, which is the middle radical (ʿayn) of the word, was dropped in all the inflections of the imperfect verb for lightness, and the rāʾ took the vowel of the hamza. The majority read the rāʾ with kasra, and it was read with sukūn, which is weak, because the kasra here indicates the omitted yāʾ. The justification of the sukūn is that the separate [sequence] was likened to the connected one, so it was made quiescent just as فَخِذٌ and كَتِفٌ are made quiescent [as فَخْذٌ and كَتْفٌ]. It is also said that the transmitter did not record the reciter accurately, because the reciter pronounced [the vowel] in a reduced, snatched way (ikhtilās), so he thought that he had made it quiescent. The singular of الْمَنَاسِكُ is مَنْسَكٌ, with fatḥa on the sīn or with kasra [مَنْسِكٌ].

ukberi-tibyan:130-130.t:
Allah the Exalted said: (وَمَنْ يَرْغَبُ عَنْ مِلَّةِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ إِلَّا مَنْ سَفِهَ نَفْسَهُ وَلَقَدِ اصْطَفَيْنَاهُ فِي الدُّنْيَا وَإِنَّهُ فِي الْآخِرَةِ لَمِنَ الصَّالِحِينَ (١٣٠)).
His saying, Exalted is He: (وَمَنْ يَرْغَبُ): مَنْ is interrogative with the sense of disavowal (inkār); that is why إِلَّا comes after it, since what is disavowed is negated. It is in the position of the nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject), and يَرْغَبُ is the khabar (predicate), containing a pronoun that refers back to مَنْ. (إِلَّا مَنْ): مَنْ is in the position of the accusative as excepted, and it may be nominative as a badal (substitute) for the pronoun in يَرْغَبُ. مَنْ is an indefinite noun qualified by an adjective, or means "the one who" (الَّذِي). And (نَفْسَهُ) is the object of سَفِهَ, because its meaning is "was ignorant of"; the implied form is: "except one who is ignorant of the creation of his soul or of its destination". It is also said that the implied form is سَفَّهَ with doubling [i.e. "made a fool of"]; and it is said that the implied form is "in himself" (فِي نَفْسِهِ). Al-Farrāʾ said it is a tamyīz (specification), but this is weak because it is definite.
(فِي الْآخِرَةِ): attached (mutaʿalliq) to الصَّالِحِينَ, i.e. "and indeed he is among the righteous in the Hereafter"; on this view the alif and lām are for definiteness, not in the sense of الَّذِي, because if you made it in the sense of الَّذِي you would have placed [part of] the ṣila (relative clause) before the relative. It is also said that it is in the sense of الَّذِي, and فِي is attached to an omitted verb that «الصَّالِحِينَ» explains, its implied form being: "indeed he is righteous in the Hereafter". This is called al-tabyīn (explication), and its parallel is:
رَبَّيْتُهُ حَتَّى إِذَا تَمَعْدَدَا كَانَ جَزَائِي بِالْعَصَا أَنْ أُجْلَدَا
("I raised him until, when he grew sturdy, my reward was to be beaten with the stick.")
Its implied form is: "my reward was the beating with the stick". This is frequent in the Quran and in poetry.

ukberi-tibyan:131-131.t:
Allah the Exalted said: (إِذْ قَالَ لَهُ رَبُّهُ أَسْلِمْ قَالَ أَسْلَمْتُ لِرَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ (١٣١)).
His saying, Exalted is He: إِذْ قَالَ لَهُ: إِذْ is an adverb of time for «اصْطَفَيْنَاهُ»; it may be a badal (substitute) for His saying فِي الدُّنْيَا; and the implied form may be: "remember when He said". (لِرَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ): what this wording would require is for him to say "I have submitted to You" (أَسْلَمْتُ لَكَ), since the Lord has already been mentioned; but he put the overt noun in the place of the pronoun out of reverence, because it contains what is not in the first wording: [the first] implies that He is his Lord, and in the second wording there is his acknowledgment that He is the Lord of all.

ukberi-tibyan:132-132.t:
Allah the Exalted said: (وَوَصَّى بِهَا إِبْرَاهِيمُ بَنِيهِ وَيَعْقُوبُ يَا بَنِيَّ إِنَّ اللَّهَ اصْطَفَى لَكُمُ الدِّينَ فَلَا تَمُوتُنَّ إِلَّا وَأَنْتُمْ مُسْلِمُونَ (١٣٢)).
His saying, Exalted is He: (وَوَصَّى بِهَا): it is read with doubling [without alif], and أَوْصَى with alif; both have one meaning. The pronoun in بِهَا refers to the religion (al-milla).
(وَيَعْقُوبُ): conjoined to إِبْرَاهِيمُ, and its object is omitted, its implied form being: "and Yaʿqūb enjoined his sons", because Yaʿqūb also enjoined his sons just as Ibrāhīm enjoined his sons; the proof of that is His saying: إِذْ قَالَ لِبَنِيهِ مَا تَعْبُدُونَ مِنْ بَعْدِي. The implied form is: "he said: O my sons". So it may be Ibrāhīm who said "O my sons".
And it may be Yaʿqūb. The alif in (اصْطَفَى) is a substitute for a yāʾ that is a substitute for a wāw; its origin is from الصَّفْوَة, and when the wāw falls in fourth position or beyond it is changed to yāʾ; that is why the alif is pronounced with imāla (inclination toward i) in cases like this.
(فَلَا تَمُوتُنَّ): the prohibition is, in wording, against dying, but in meaning it is about something else; the implied form is: "do not part from Islam until you die". وَأَنْتُمْ مُسْلِمُونَ is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial), and what governs it is the verb before إِلَّا.

ukberi-tibyan:78-78.t:
Allah the Exalted said: (وَمِنْهُمْ أُمِّيُّونَ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ الْكِتَابَ إِلَّا أَمَانِيَّ وَإِنْ هُمْ إِلَّا يَظُنُّونَ (٧٨)).
His saying, the Exalted: (أُمِّيُّونَ): a mubtadaʾ (subject), and what precedes it is the khabar (predicate). On the doctrine of al-Akhfash, it may be made nominative by the adverbial phrase (al-ẓarf). (لَا يَعْلَمُونَ): in the position of the nominative as an adjective of أُمِّيُّونَ.
(إِلَّا أَمَانِيَّ): a disjoined exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ), because wishful fancies (al-amānī) are not of the genus of knowledge. The implied sense of إِلَّا in the like of this is لَكِنْ ("but"), i.e. "but they wish it as fancies". The singular of الْأَمَانِيُّ is أُمْنِيَّةٌ; the yāʾ is doubled in both the singular and the plural, and it may be lightened in both.
(وَإِنْ هُمْ): إِنْ means مَا ("not"), but it does not govern as مَا governs. It most often comes in that sense when the negation is broken by إِلَّا; it has also come without إِلَّا with it, and that will be mentioned in its place. The implied form is: "they are nothing but a people who conjecture (وَإِنْ هُمْ إِلَّا قَوْمٌ يَظُنُّونَ)".

ukberi-tibyan:79-79.t:
Allah the Exalted said: (فَوَيْلٌ لِلَّذِينَ يَكْتُبُونَ الْكِتَابَ بِأَيْدِيهِمْ ثُمَّ يَقُولُونَ هَذَا مِنْ عِنْدِ اللَّهِ لِيَشْتَرُوا بِهِ ثَمَنًا قَلِيلًا فَوَيْلٌ لَهُمْ مِمَّا كَتَبَتْ أَيْدِيهِمْ وَوَيْلٌ لَهُمْ مِمَّا يَكْسِبُونَ (٧٩)).
His saying, the Exalted: (فَوَيْلٌ لِلَّذِينَ يَكْتُبُونَ): a mubtadaʾ (subject) and a khabar (predicate). Had it been put in the accusative, that would have a justification, the implied form being "Allah has imposed woe upon them (أَلْزَمَهُمُ اللَّهُ وَيْلًا)", with the lām for clarification (li-l-tabyīn), because the noun was not mentioned before the maṣdar (verbal noun).
And الْوَيْلُ is a maṣdar from which no verb is used, because its first radical and its second radical are both weak.
His saying, the Exalted: (الْكِتَابَ): a mafʿūl bihi (direct object), i.e. "what is written"; it is weak for it to be a maṣdar. The mention of the hands is emphasis. Their singular is يَدٌ, whose original form is يَدْيٌ, like فَلْسٌ. This plural is a plural of paucity (jamʿ qilla), and its original form is أَيْدُيٌ with a ḍamma on the dāl; a ḍamma before a yāʾ is felt to be heavy, especially with a vowelled yāʾ, so the ḍamma was turned into a kasra and it joined the defective nouns (al-manqūṣ). (لِيَشْتَرُوا): the lām is attached (mutaʿalliq) to (يَقُولُونَ). (مِمَّا كَتَبَتْ أَيْدِيهِمْ): مَا means "that which", or it is an indefinite noun qualified by an adjective (nakira mawṣūfa), or it is maṣdariyya (forming a verbal noun); and likewise (مِمَّا يَكْسِبُونَ).

ukberi-tibyan:80-80.t:
Allah the Exalted said: (وَقَالُوا لَنْ تَمَسَّنَا النَّارُ إِلَّا أَيَّامًا مَعْدُودَةً قُلْ أَتَّخَذْتُمْ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ عَهْدًا فَلَنْ يُخْلِفَ اللَّهُ عَهْدَهُ أَمْ تَقُولُونَ عَلَى اللَّهِ مَا لَا تَعْلَمُونَ (٨٠)).
His saying, the Exalted: (إِلَّا أَيَّامًا): accusative as an adverbial (ẓarf), and إِلَّا has no governing effect on it, because the verb did not pass to an adverbial before this adverbial. The original form of أَيَّامٌ is أَيْوَامٌ; when the yāʾ and the wāw came together and the first of them preceded with quiescence, the wāw was changed into a yāʾ and the yāʾ was assimilated into the yāʾ, for lightness.
(أَتَّخَذْتُمْ): the hamza is for interrogation, and the connecting hamza (hamzat al-waṣl) is omitted, being dispensed with by the interrogative hamza. It has the sense of جَعَلْتُمْ ("you have made") that is transitive to a single object.
(فَلَنْ يُخْلِفَ): the implied form is: "so that they may say: He will never break (فَيَقُولُوا لَنْ يُخْلِفَ)".
(مَا لَا تَعْلَمُونَ): مَا means "that which", or it is indefinite; it cannot be maṣdariyya (forming a verbal noun) here.

ukberi-tibyan:81-81.t:
Allah the Exalted said: (بَلَى مَنْ كَسَبَ سَيِّئَةً وَأَحَاطَتْ بِهِ خَطِيئَتُهُ فَأُولَئِكَ أَصْحَابُ النَّارِ هُمْ فِيهَا خَالِدُونَ (٨١)).
His saying, the Exalted: (بَلَى): a particle by which the one answering affirms the negated statement before it. You say: "Did Zayd not come? (أَمَا جَاءَ زَيْدٌ؟)", and the one answering says: بَلَى, i.e. "he did come". For this reason it is correct to bring an affirmative statement after بَلَى, so you say: "بَلَى, قَدْ جَاءَ". If you say in answer to a negation نَعَمْ, it is an acknowledgment of the negation, and it is correct to bring the negation after it, as when one says: "Did Zayd not come? (مَا جَاءَ زَيْدٌ؟)", and you say: "نَعَمْ, مَا جَاءَ" ("Yes, he did not come").
The yāʾ [i.e. the final alif maqṣūra] is part of the particle itself. The Kufans said: it is بَلْ, to which the yāʾ was added; and that is weak.
(مَنْ كَسَبَ): there are two views on «مَنْ». The first: it means "the one who" (al-ladhī). The second: it is conditional. On both views it is a mubtadaʾ (subject). «إِلَّا أَنْ كَسَبَ» [Translator's note: so printed; the sense requires إِلَّا أَنَّ «كَسَبَ», i.e. "except that كَسَبَ"] has no grammatical position if مَنْ is a relative, and has a position if it is conditional. The apodosis is: فَأُولَئِكَ, which is a mubtadaʾ, and (أَصْحَابُ النَّارِ) is its khabar (predicate); and the clause is the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ), or the khabar of مَنْ.
And السَّيِّئَةُ is on the pattern فَيْعِلَةٌ, like سَيِّدٌ and هَيِّنٌ; we have mentioned that at His saying: (أَوْ كَصَيِّبٍ). The second radical (ʿayn) of the word is a wāw, because it is from سَاءَهُ يَسُوءُهُ.
(بِهِ): it refers back to the wording of مَنْ, and the plural after it refers back to its meaning. And what indicates that «مَنْ» means "the one who" is the conjoined [clause], namely His saying: (وَالَّذِينَ آمَنُوا).

ukberi-tibyan:83-83.t:
Allah the Exalted said: (وَإِذْ أَخَذْنَا مِيثَاقَ بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ لَا تَعْبُدُونَ إِلَّا اللَّهَ وَبِالْوَالِدَيْنِ إِحْسَانًا وَذِي الْقُرْبَى وَالْيَتَامَى وَالْمَسَاكِينِ وَقُولُوا لِلنَّاسِ حُسْنًا وَأَقِيمُوا الصَّلَاةَ وَآتُوا الزَّكَاةَ ثُمَّ تَوَلَّيْتُمْ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا مِنْكُمْ وَأَنْتُمْ مُعْرِضُونَ (٨٣)).
His saying, the Exalted: (لَا تَعْبُدُونَ إِلَّا اللَّهَ): it is read with the tāʾ, on the implied form "We said to them: you shall not worship (قُلْنَا لَهُمْ لَا تَعْبُدُونَ)", and with the yāʾ, because بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ is an overt noun, so the pronoun and the imperfect prefix are in the form of the absent (third person), since overt nouns are all third person. There are four views on its i'rab:
The first: that it is the answer to an oath indicated by the meaning, namely His saying: «أَخَذْنَا مِيثَاقَ», because its meaning is "We made them swear", or "We said to them: by Allah, you shall not worship". The second: that «أَنْ» is intended, the implied form being: "We took the covenant of the Children of Israel that you should not worship any but Allah (عَلَى أَنْ لَا تَعْبُدُوا إِلَّا اللَّهَ)"; then the preposition was omitted, then أَنْ was omitted, so the verb became nominative. Its parallel is:
أَلَا أَيُّهَذَا الزَّاجِرِي أَحْضُرُ الْوَغَى
("O you who rebuke me for attending the battle")
with the nominative, the implied form being "from that I attend (عَنْ أَنْ أَحْضُرَ)". The third: that it is in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial), its implied form being "We took their covenant, they being affirmers of Allah's oneness (مُوَحِّدِينَ)". It is a concomitant ḥāl (ḥāl muṣāḥiba) and an anticipated one (muqaddara), because at the time the covenant was taken they were affirmers of oneness, and they committed themselves to continue in affirming oneness. If you made it a concomitant ḥāl only, the implied form being "We took their covenant, they committing themselves to remaining in affirming oneness", that would be permissible; and if you made it an anticipated ḥāl only, it would be permissible, the implied form being "We took their covenant, they intending to affirm oneness forever as long as they lived".
The fourth view: that its wording is the wording of a statement while its meaning is prohibition, the implied form being: "We said to them: do not worship (لَا تَعْبُدُوا)". There is a fifth view in it: that the ḥāl is omitted, the implied form being "We took their covenant, saying such-and-such"; the omission of "saying" is frequent. Like that is His saying, the Exalted: (وَإِذْ أَخَذْنَا مِيثَاقَكُمْ لَا تَسْفِكُونَ).
(إِلَّا اللَّهَ): the object of تَعْبُدُونَ; إِلَّا has no part in making it accusative, except that the verb before it had not taken its object in full. (وَبِالْوَالِدَيْنِ إِحْسَانًا): إِحْسَانًا is a maṣdar (verbal noun), i.e. "and We said: be good to the parents with goodness (أَحْسِنُوا بِالْوَالِدَيْنِ إِحْسَانًا)". It may also be a mafʿūl bihi (direct object), the implied form being "and We said: take as a charge, regarding the parents, goodness (اسْتَوْصُوا بِالْوَالِدَيْنِ إِحْسَانًا)". It may also be a mafʿūl lahu (object of purpose), i.e. "and We enjoined them concerning the parents for the sake of being good to them".
(وَذِي الْقُرْبَى): ذِي is singular here only because He intended the genus; or the singular has been put in place of the plural, and its parallel has already been mentioned. (وَالْيَتَامَى): plural of يَتِيمٌ; the plural of فَعِيلٌ on فَعَالَى is rare.
The mīm in (وَالْمَسَاكِينِ) is redundant (zāʾida), because it is from al-sukūn (stillness).
(وَقُولُوا): i.e. "and We said to them: say".
(حُسْنًا): it is read with a ḍamma on the ḥāʾ and a sukūn on the sīn, and with a fatḥa on both; they are two dialectal forms, like الْعُرْبُ and الْعَرَبُ, and الْحُزْنُ and الْحَزَنُ. Some distinguished between them, saying: the fatḥa reading is an adjective of an omitted maṣdar, i.e. "a good speech (قَوْلًا حَسَنًا)", and the ḍamma reading is on the assumption that a muḍāf is omitted, i.e. "a speech possessing goodness (قَوْلًا ذَا حُسْنٍ)".
It was also read with a ḍamma on the ḥāʾ without tanwīn [i.e. حُسْنَى], the alif being for the feminine.
(إِلَّا قَلِيلًا مِنْكُمْ): the accusative is as a joined exception (istithnāʾ muttaṣil), and that is the [proper] way.
It was read with the nominative as an anomalous reading (shādhdh); its justification is that it is [the agent] of an omitted verb, as though He said: "a few refrained". It cannot be a badal (substitute), because the meaning would become: "then a few turned away". It may be a mubtadaʾ (subject) with an omitted khabar (predicate), i.e. "except a few of you did not turn away", just as they said: "I passed by no one but that a man of Banū Tamīm was better than him (مَا مَرَرْتُ بِأَحَدٍ إِلَّا وَرَجُلٌ مِنْ بَنِي تَمِيمٍ خَيْرٌ مِنْهُ)". It may also be a tawkīd (emphasis) of the nominative pronoun from which the exception is made; Sībawayh and his followers call it a naʿt and a waṣf (description). Abū ʿAlī cited, for the like of the nominative in this verse:
وَبِالصَّرِيمَةِ مِنْهُمْ مَنْزِلٌ خَلَقٌ ... عَافٍ تَغَيَّرَ إِلَّا النُّؤْيُ وَالْوَتِدُ
("At al-Ṣarīma they have a worn, effaced dwelling, all changed except the trench and the tent-peg")
(وَأَنْتُمْ مُعْرِضُونَ): a clause in the position of a corroborative ḥāl (ḥāl muʾakkida), because تَوَلَّيْتُمْ makes it unnecessary.
It is also said that the meaning is: "you turned away with your bodies while you were averse with your hearts"; on this view it is a transitional ḥāl (ḥāl muntaqila). And it is said that تَوَلَّيْتُمْ refers to their forefathers and وَأَنْتُمْ مُعْرِضُونَ refers to themselves, as He said: (وَإِذْ نَجَّيْنَاكُمْ مِنْ آلِ فِرْعَوْنَ), meaning their forefathers.

ukberi-tibyan:38-38.t:
Allah the Exalted says: (قُلْنَا اهْبِطُوا مِنْهَا جَمِيعًا فَإِمَّا يَأْتِيَنَّكُمْ مِنِّي هُدًى فَمَنْ تَبِعَ هُدَايَ فَلَا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ وَلَا هُمْ يَحْزَنُونَ (٣٨)).
His saying: (مِنْهَا جَمِيعًا): a ḥāl (circumstantial), i.e. "all together", whether at a single time or at [different] times, in such a way that they share in the descent. (فَإِمَّا): إن is a conditional particle and ما is a particle emphasizing it. And (يَأْتِيَنَّكُمْ) is the protasis (fiʿl al-sharṭ), emphasized with the heavy nūn, and with it the verb always becomes indeclinable (mabnī).
Every conditional verb in the Qur'an that follows إمّا is emphasized with the nūn, and that is the regular rule, because the addition of ما signals the intent of strong emphasis; in poetry it has occurred without being emphasized with the nūn.
The apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) is: فمن تبع together with its own apodosis. من is in the position of the nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject), and the khabar (predicate) is تبع, which contains an agent pronoun referring to من; the position of تبع is jussive by من, and the apodosis is: فلا خوف عليهم.
Likewise, every noun with which you make a condition and which is a mubtadaʾ has the protasis as its khabar, not the apodosis; for this reason it must contain a pronoun referring to the mubtadaʾ, while that pronoun is not required in the apodosis. Thus if you said من يقم أكرم زيدا ("whoever stands, I will honour Zayd") it would be permissible, but if you said من يقم زيدا أكرمه ("whoever stands, Zayd — I will honour him"), referring the hāʾ to من, it would not be permissible.
Some held that the khabar is the protasis and the apodosis together; and it has been said that the khabar is whichever of the two contains a pronoun referring to من. And (خَوْفٌ) is a mubtadaʾ and عليهم is the khabar; starting with an indefinite noun is allowed because of the sense of generality it has through the negation in it.
The nominative with tanwīn here is preferable to indeclinability on fatḥa for two reasons. First: that something was conjoined to it in which only the nominative is permissible, namely His saying: ولا هم, because it is definite and لا does not govern definite nouns; so it is better to make what it is conjoined to the same, so that the two clauses match, as they said regarding a verb occupied with the agent pronoun, as in قام زيد وعمرا كلمته ("Zayd stood, and ʿAmr, I spoke to him"): the accusative in عمرو is preferable so that it is made accusative by a verb, just as the verb governed what it is conjoined to.
The second reason is from the side of meaning: indeclinability indicates the negation of fear from them completely, and that is not what is meant; rather what is meant is its negation from them in the Hereafter.
If it is said: why is the reason for the nominative not that this speech is mentioned as the recompense of those who follow the guidance, and it is not fitting to negate slight fear from them and leave the impression that much fear is established?
It is answered: with the nominative, the negation of much may be implied, its implied form being: "no great fear is upon them", which would leave the impression that a little is established; that is the opposite of what was supposed in the question. So it is clear that the reason for the nominative is what we mentioned.
(هُدَايَ): the well-known reading keeps the alif before the yāʾ, following the singular form before iḍāfa.
It is also read هُدَيَّ, with a doubled yāʾ; its rationale is that the letter before the yāʾ of the first person is given kasra in a sound noun, and the alif cannot take kasra, so it was changed into a yāʾ, which is of the same kind as the kasra, and then assimilated.

ukberi-tibyan:39-39.t:
Allah the Exalted says: (وَالَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا وَكَذَّبُوا بِآيَاتِنَا أُولَئِكَ أَصْحَابُ النَّارِ هُمْ فِيهَا خَالِدُونَ) ((٣٩)).
His saying: (بِآيَاتِنَا): the original form of آية is أيّة, because its first radical (fāʾ) is a hamza and its second and third radicals (ʿayn and lām) are two yāʾs, since it is from تأيّا القوم, when the people gathered. [Translator's note: the Arabic text prints «تَأَتَّى» here; the sense of gathering suggests تأيّا, but the text is translated as given.] They said in the plural آياء, in which the first yāʾ appears; the final hamza replaces a yāʾ, its pattern is أفعال, and the second alif is changed from a hamza which is the first radical of the word. If its second radical were wāw, they would have said آواء. Then they changed the quiescent yāʾ in أيّة into an alif contrary to the regular rule; similar to it are غاية and ثاية. It has also been said: its original form is أيِيَة, then the first yāʾ was changed into an alif because it was vowelled and preceded by fatḥa.
It has also been said: its original form is أيَيَة, with fatḥa on the first and second, then what we mentioned was done to the yāʾ. Both views are open to objection, because the rule for two yāʾs when they come together in such a case is that the second is changed, because of its nearness to the end [of the word].
It has also been said: its original form is آيِيَة on the pattern فاعلة, and the regular rule would be for it to be assimilated, so that one says آيّة like دابّة, except that it was lightened, as كيّنونة was lightened to كينونة; but this is weak, because the lightening in that form was due to the length of the word. (أُولَئِكَ) is a mubtadaʾ (subject), and «أصحاب النار» is its khabar (predicate). And «هم فيها خالدون» is a mubtadaʾ and khabar in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial) from أصحاب.
It has also been said that it may be a ḥāl from النار, because the clause contains a pronoun referring to it; the operator in the ḥāl would then be the meaning of the iḍāfa, or the implied lām.

ukberi-tibyan:40-40.t:
Allah the Exalted says: (يَا بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ اذْكُرُوا نِعْمَتِيَ الَّتِي أَنْعَمْتُ عَلَيْكُمْ وَأَوْفُوا بِعَهْدِي أُوفِ بِعَهْدِكُمْ وَإِيَّايَ فَارْهَبُونِ (٤٠)).
His saying, Exalted is He: (يَا بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ): إسرائيل is a diptote because it is a foreign proper name. The Arabs have pronounced it in various dialectal forms: some say إسرائيل, with a hamza followed by a yāʾ followed by a lām; some say the same but change the hamza into a yāʾ; some keep the hamza and omit the yāʾ; some omit both and say إسرال; and some say إسراين, with nūn.
And (بَنِي) is the plural of ابن, given the sound plural, though it is not truly sound, because the form of its singular is not preserved in its plural. The original singular is بنَو on the pattern فعَل, with a vowel on the second radical, because of their saying أبناء in the plural, like جبل and أجبال. Its last radical is wāw; some said its last radical is yāʾ, and البنوّة is no proof [for wāw], since they have said الفتوّة, which is from [a root with] yāʾ.
(أَنْعَمْتُ عَلَيْكُمْ): the original form is أنعمت بها, so that the pronoun refers back to the relative noun; the preposition was omitted and it became أنعمتها, then the pronoun was omitted, as it was omitted in His saying (أَهَذَا الَّذِي بَعَثَ اللَّهُ رَسُولًا). (وَأَوْفُوا): in the past tense one says وفى and وفّى, and on this basis it has been read: (أُوفِ بِعَهْدِكُمْ), with the fāʾ without and with doubling. (وَإِيَّايَ): accusative by an omitted verb indicated by فارهبون, its implied form being: "and dread Me, so dread Me". It is not permissible for it to be accusative by (ارهبون), because that has already taken its object.

ukberi-tibyan:41-41.t:
Allah the Exalted says: (وَآمِنُوا بِمَا أَنْزَلْتُ مُصَدِّقًا لِمَا مَعَكُمْ وَلَا تَكُونُوا أَوَّلَ كَافِرٍ بِهِ وَلَا تَشْتَرُوا بِآيَاتِي ثَمَنًا قَلِيلًا وَإِيَّايَ فَاتَّقُونِ) ((٤١)).
His saying: (مُصَدِّقًا): an emphatic ḥāl (circumstantial) from the omitted hāʾ in أنزلت.
And (مَعَكُمْ) is accusative as an adverbial (ẓarf), its operator being the [implied] istiqrār.
(أَوَّلَ): it is أفعل; its first and second radicals (fāʾ and ʿayn) are both wāw according to Sībawayh, and no verb is formed from it because of the weakness of the fāʾ and the ʿayn. Its feminine is أُولى, and its original form is وُولى; the wāw was changed to hamza because it had a permanent ḍamma, and it was not left in the original form, as وُقّتت and وجوه were, out of dislike for two wāws coming together.
Some of the Kufans said: the origin of the word is from وأل يئل, when one escapes; so its original form is أوأل, then the hamza was lightened by being changed into a wāw, and then the first [wāw] was assimilated into it. This is not regular; rather, the regular way of lightening such a hamza is to cast its vowel onto the quiescent letter before it and omit it.
Some of them said: it is from آل يؤول; so the original form of the word is أأول, then the second hamza was moved back and placed after the wāw, and then what was done in the preceding view was done to it, so its pattern now is أعفل.
(كَافِرٍ): its form is singular, but it has the meaning of the plural, i.e. "the first of the disbelievers", as one says هو أحسن رجل ("he is the best of men"). It has also been said that the implied form is: "the first disbelieving group".

ukberi-tibyan:42-42.t:
Allah the Exalted says: (وَلَا تَلْبِسُوا الْحَقَّ بِالْبَاطِلِ وَتَكْتُمُوا الْحَقَّ وَأَنْتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ) ((٤٢)).
His saying, Exalted is He: (وَتَكْتُمُوا الْحَقَّ): it is jussive by conjunction with ولا تلبسوا; it may also be accusative as an answer with the wāw, i.e. "do not combine the two", as in your saying لا تأكل السمك وتشربَ اللبن ("do not eat fish and drink milk [together]"). (وَأَنْتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ): in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial), its operator being لا تلبسوا and تكتموا.

ukberi-tibyan:43-43.t:
Allah the Exalted says: (وَأَقِيمُوا الصَّلَاةَ وَآتُوا الزَّكَاةَ وَارْكَعُوا مَعَ الرَّاكِعِينَ (٤٣)).
His saying, Exalted is He: (وَأَقِيمُوا الصَّلَاةَ): the original form of أقيموا is أقْوِموا, and what we mentioned regarding His saying ويقيمون الصلاة at the beginning of the sūra was done to it. (وَآتُوا الزَّكَاةَ): its original form is آتِيُوا; the ḍamma on the yāʾ was found heavy, so it was made quiescent and omitted because of the meeting of two quiescent letters, then the tāʾ was given the vowel of the omitted yāʾ. It has also been said that it was given ḍamma to harmonize with the wāw, as it was given ḍamma in اضربوا and the like. The alif of الزكاة is converted from a wāw, because of their saying زكا الشيء يزكو ("the thing grew"), and they said زكوات in the plural.
(مَعَ الرَّاكِعِينَ): an adverbial (ẓarf).

ukberi-tibyan:3-3.t:
Allah the Exalted said: (الَّذِينَ يُؤْمِنُونَ بِالْغَيْبِ وَيُقِيمُونَ الصَّلَاةَ وَمِمَّا رَزَقْنَاهُمْ يُنْفِقُونَ (٣)).
His saying, the Exalted: (الَّذِينَ يُؤْمِنُونَ) is in the position of the genitive as a naʿt (adjective) of الْمُتَّقِينَ. It may also be in the position of the accusative, either following the position of لِلْمُتَّقِينَ or by implying أَعْنِي ("I mean").
It may also be in the position of the nominative by implying "they are" (هُمْ), or as a mubtadaʾ (subject) whose khabar (predicate) is (أُولَئِكَ عَلَى هُدًى). The original form of (يُؤْمِنُونَ) is يُؤَأْمِنُونَ, because it is from al-amn (security), and its past tense is آمَنَ. The alif [in آمَنَ] is a substitute for a quiescent hamza that was turned into an alif out of dislike for two hamzas coming together; nowhere did they pronounce the second one fully, because it is quiescent and the letter before it has fatḥa. Its counterpart among nouns is آدَمُ and آخَرُ.
As for the imperfect, you do not combine the two hamzas that are original, because that would lead you, in the first person, to three hamzas: the first is the hamza of the imperfect prefix; the second is the hamza of afʿala that is in آمَنَ; and the third is the hamza that is the first radical of the word. So they dropped the middle one, as they dropped it in أُكْرِمُ, so that the hamzas would not come together. Dropping the middle one was more appropriate than dropping the first, because the first is a particle carrying meaning; and [more appropriate than the view of] whoever dropped the third, because the third is the first radical of the word, while the middle one is extra [Translator's note: the sentence in the text is elliptical: «وَمَنْ حَذَفَ الثَّالِثَةَ: لِأَنَّ الثَّالِثَةَ فَاءُ الْكَلِمَةِ»; the bracketed words are supplied to make the argument read].
If you want to make that clear, say: آمَنَ has four letters, so it is like دَحْرَجَ. If you said أُدَحْرِجُ, you would bring all that was in the past tense and add to it the hamza of the speaker; the like of this must hold in أُومِنُ. So of the hamzas, what remains is the first; the wāw after it is substituted for the quiescent hamza that is the first radical of the word; and the middle hamza is the one dropped. The quiescent hamza was turned into wāw only because it is quiescent and the letter before it has ḍamma. When you say نُؤْمِنُ, تُؤْمِنُ and يُؤْمِنُ, two ways are open to you. First: the hamza, according to the original.
Second: turning the hamza into wāw for lightness. The middle hamza was dropped by analogy with أُومِنُ; the original is يُؤَأْمِنُ. As for أُومِنُ, the second [hamza] may not be pronounced as hamza in any case, for the reason we mentioned.
(الْغَيْبِ) here is a maṣdar (verbal noun) with the meaning of the active participle, i.e. "they believe in what is absent (الْغَائِبِ) from them".
It may also have the meaning of the passive participle, i.e. الْمَغِيبُ ("what is hidden"), as in His saying (هَذَا خَلْقُ اللَّهِ), i.e. what He has created; and "a dirham, the striking of the emir" (دِرْهَمٌ ضَرْبُ الْأَمِيرِ), i.e. struck by him.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: (وَيُقِيمُونَ): its original form is يُؤَقْوِمُونَ; its past tense is أَقَامَ, and its second radical is wāw, because you say يَقُومُ from it. The hamza was dropped as it was dropped in أُقِيمُ because of two hamzas coming together; and likewise in everything that has an imperfect prefix, so that the paradigm of the imperfect verbs would not vary. As for the wāw, the same was done to it as was done in نَسْتَعِينُ, which we have mentioned. The alif of الصَّلَاةِ is converted from a wāw, because you say صَلَوَاتٌ. الصَّلَاةُ is the maṣdar of صَلَّى; what is meant by it here is the specific acts and sayings [of the prayer], and for that reason it is treated like nouns that are not verbal nouns.
His saying, the Exalted: (وَمِمَّا رَزَقْنَاهُمْ): مِنْ is attached (mutaʿalliq) to (يُنْفِقُونَ), the implied order being وَيُنْفِقُونَ مِمَّا رَزَقْنَاهُمْ, so that the verb comes before the object, just as His sayings (يُؤْمِنُونَ) and (يُقِيمُونَ) are. The verb was placed after the object only so that the verse-endings would agree. مَا has the meaning of الَّذِي. رَزَقْنَا is transitive to two objects; the second of them has been omitted here, and it is what refers back to مَا, its implied form being رَزَقْنَاهُمُوهُ or رَزَقْنَاهُمْ إِيَّاهُ.
مَا may also be an indefinite noun described [by what follows], with the meaning of "a thing", i.e. "and from wealth which We provided them"; then رَزَقْنَاهُمْ is in the position of the genitive as an adjective of مَا.
